docs.title: Breaks
docs.text:
srs.breaks

Script/plugin-facing surface for the BreakManager — schedule, observe, and react to break cycles (work → request → logout → idle → login → recover).

Credentials are sandboxed

Scripts can not see or set credentials — those are owned by the launcher and the client. Scripts can only observe state, request/skip breaks, and subscribe to phase events.

Auto-pause / resume

The Scheduler pauses scripts during a break; their pulse / onTick callbacks just stop firing. Scripts don't need to call setPaused on themselves.

Logout during breaks is the default

logoutDuringBreak now defaults to true: the scheduler logs the account out for the break and logs back in when it ends. Set it to false in the profile to idle in place instead. Because setProfile is declarative, a script that calls it without this key gets the logout behaviour.

docs.title: Lifecycle control
docs.text:
Method Lua Start the scheduler srs.breaks.start() Stop the scheduler srs.breaks.stop() Request a break now (optional minutes; -1 = profile-driven) srs.breaks.requestBreakNow(minutes?) Skip the next scheduled break (one-shot) srs.breaks.skipNextBreak() Recover from a failed login cycle srs.breaks.resetFromFailed() Hop to a world after each relogin (0 / -1 = off) srs.breaks.setHopWorld(world)

setHopWorld makes the BreakManager hop to a different world when it logs back in after a break; a 0 / negative value disables hopping.

docs.title: State queries
docs.text: Method Lua Current Phase enum srs.breaks.phase() → int Human-readable phase name srs.breaks.phaseName() → string Last login-failure reason srs.breaks.lastFailureReason() → int Last failure name srs.breaks.failureName() → string Seconds until next break srs.breaks.secondsUntilBreak() → int Seconds remaining in current break srs.breaks.secondsRemainingInBreak() → int Daily play time so far (seconds) srs.breaks.dailyPlaySecondsAccumulated() → int

docs.title: Break handshake
docs.text:
For scripts that need to reach a safe state (banked, out of combat, etc.) before they get paused:

  1. Call declareBreakAware() once (from onTick / pulse) to register as a script the Scheduler will wait on.
  2. Check isBreakRequested() each tick during normal work.
  3. Once safe, call signalReady() — idempotent, fine every tick.
Method Lua Has a break been requested? srs.breaks.isBreakRequested() → bool Opt this script into the wait set srs.breaks.declareBreakAware() Mark this script ready for break srs.breaks.signalReady()

Caller attribution + no grace timeout

Handshake calls must be made from inside an onTick / pulse / draw callback — the Scheduler reads the currently-firing script index for attribution. Calls from outside any callback (e.g. top-level chunk during loadFile) won't attribute correctly and are silently dropped.

There is no grace timeout: a script that opts in but never signals will block every future break. Don't declareBreakAware unless you intend to signal.

docs.title: Profile
docs.text:
Timing-only (no credential fields).

Method Lua Read srs.breaks.getProfile() → table Write (declarative — omitted keys reset to defaults) srs.breaks.setProfile(table)

setProfile is declarative

setProfile does not merge into the current profile: any key you omit from the table resets to its default (the column below), not to its previously-set value. A script calling srs.breaks.setProfile({workMinutesMin = 40}) silently resets everything else — including logoutDuringBreak — back to defaults. To tweak one field, read getProfile(), mutate the returned table, and pass the whole table back:

local p = srs.breaks.getProfile()
p.workMinutesMin = 40
srs.breaks.setProfile(p)

Profile fields:

Field Default Notes workMinutesMin 25 Min work segment workMinutesMax 55 Max work segment workSecondsMin 0 Sub-minute work override — when either bound is > 0 it takes precedence over the work-minutes pair workSecondsMax 0 Upper bound of the work-seconds override breakMinutesMin 5 Min break length breakMinutesMax 20 Max break length breakSecondsMin 0 Sub-minute break override — when either bound is > 0 it takes precedence over the break-minutes pair breakSecondsMax 0 Upper bound of the break-seconds override logoutDuringBreak true Logout vs. idle-in-place. Defaults to logging out for the break and logging back in when it ends; set false to idle in place instead. maxLoginRetries 4 Login retry budget loginRetryBaseSeconds 5 Exponential backoff base enableLoginWatchdog true Watchdog on login transition loginWatchdogTimeoutMinutes 10 Watchdog timeout extendedSleepDurationMinutes 30 After failure

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Each subscriber returns an integer handle; pass it to unsubscribe to remove.

Method Lua Phase change (from, to) srs.breaks.onPhaseChange(function(from, to) end) → int Break requested (entry to BreakRequested) srs.breaks.onBreakRequested(function() end) → int Before logout (entry to BreakPending) srs.breaks.onBeforeLogout(function() end) → int After successful login srs.breaks.onAfterLogin(function() end) → int Login failed (reason, detail) srs.breaks.onLoginFailed(function(reason, detail) end) → int Remove subscription srs.breaks.unsubscribe(handle)

Lua subscriptions are cleaned up for you

Subscriptions made from Lua are tracked by the client and dropped automatically when the script engine is rebuilt (for example when a script is disabled and re-enabled), so a stale callback is never invoked. Calling unsubscribe(handle) removes one early; re-register your handlers when the script is installed again.

Callbacks run asynchronously

Break callbacks are queued and run on the script thread shortly after the change happens, so srs.breaks.phase() may already have moved past the to value a handler receives. Keep handlers light.

docs.title: Enums
docs.text:
Phase (srs.breaks.phase() returns an int). Lua exposes the named values as the srs.breaks.Phase.* sub-table (srs.breaks.Phase.Running, srs.breaks.Phase.Idle, ...):

Value Name Meaning 0 Stopped Scheduler not running 1 Running Normal work segment 2 BreakRequested Waiting on opted-in scripts to signalReady 3 BreakPending Ready to log out 4 LoggingOut Logout in flight 5 Idle In-break 6 LoggingIn Login in flight 7 Recovering Post-login recovery 8 ExtendedSleep Extended sleep after repeated failure 9 Failed Login failed — needs resetFromFailed

FailureReason:

Value Name 0 None 1 AuthFailed 2 Banned 3 NotMember 4 NoCredentials 5 MaxRetriesExceeded 6 WatchdogTimeout 7 Unknown

There is no srs.breaks.FailureReason Lua table — only the Phase sub-table exists. Lua scripts compare srs.breaks.lastFailureReason() against the numeric values above (or use failureName() for display).

docs.title: Example — break-aware fishing script
docs.text:
script.onTick(function()
    srs.breaks.declareBreakAware()
    if srs.breaks.isBreakRequested() and atSafeState() then
        srs.breaks.signalReady()
        return
    end
    doFishingWork()
end)

-- Optional: log every phase transition
local handle = srs.breaks.onPhaseChange(function(from, to)
    print("phase " .. from .. " → " .. to)
end)
-- Later: srs.breaks.unsubscribe(handle)

docs.title: Camera
docs.text:
srs.camera

Camera facade: read pitch / yaw / zoom and rotate or zoom the view. rotateTo* snaps instantly by writing the engine's target angles, keyboardRotateTo* drives human-looking arrow-key holds, and setZoom converges by injecting WM_MOUSEWHEEL events.

docs.title: Rotation modes
docs.text:
Three "modes" are exposed via three method families:

Family Mechanism Notes rotateTo* Direct write of the target pitch / yaw Instant, no smoothing (use easeToYaw for a smooth yaw turn). Cheap and reliable. Default. keyboardRotateTo* Arrow-key holds Slower, human-looking. For antiban scenarios. mouseRotateTo* Scroll-wheel rotation OSRS scroll is bound to zoom, not yaw, so this falls back to the direct write path on this client.

Hold duration on keyboardRotateTo* is proportional to angle delta; capped at ~2.5 s per call so a runaway rotation doesn't lock the keyboard for the script.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
Name Value Meaning Lowest pitch (srs.camera.getLowestPitch()) 128 Lowest pitch (nearly horizontal) Highest pitch 383 Highest pitch (top-down) Yaw range 2048 2048 units = 360°

CameraMode enum (registered at Lua global as CameraMode.*):

Lua const Notes CameraMode.MouseOrKeyboard Default — direct write CameraMode.MouseOnly Scroll / middle-drag (middle-drag is TODO) CameraMode.KeyboardOnly Arrow-key holds

setCameraMode only records the value (readable via getCameraMode); it does not reroute the rotateTo* family. Pick the path by calling the rotateTo*, mouseRotateTo* or keyboardRotateTo* method you want.

docs.title: State getters
docs.text:
Method Lua Pitch srs.camera.getPitch() → int Yaw srs.camera.getYaw() → int Scene-fine X srs.camera.getX() → int Scene-fine Y (vertical) srs.camera.getY() → int Scene-fine Z srs.camera.getZ() → int Current zoom (normalized to [330, 3000]) srs.camera.getZoom() → int Min zoom srs.camera.getMinZoom() → int Max zoom srs.camera.getMaxZoom() → int Lowest pitch constant srs.camera.getLowestPitch() → int Current camera mode srs.camera.getCameraMode() → CameraMode Set camera mode srs.camera.setCameraMode(m)

How zoom works

OSRS has no user-zoom integer — camera distance derives from pitch + viewport. getZoom returns a value normalized to the [330, 3000] range, and setZoom reaches a target by injecting WM_MOUSEWHEEL events (see Zoom below). Convergence is best-effort: setZoom returns false if it can't settle within tolerance.

docs.title: Rotation (default — direct write)
docs.text:
All rotateTo* calls clamp pitch to [128, 383] and wrap yaw into 0..2047 before writing. Return true on a successful write, false if the camera state isn't resolved or the write faults.

Method Lua Both axes srs.camera.rotateTo(yaw, pitch) → bool Yaw only srs.camera.rotateToYaw(yaw) → bool Yaw only, smooth srs.camera.easeToYaw(yaw) → bool Pitch only srs.camera.rotateToPitch(pitch) → bool Face a tile srs.camera.rotateToTile(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → bool Face an entity srs.camera.rotateToEntity(target) → bool

easeToYaw sets only the engine's target yaw (masked to 0..2047) and lets the game's own follow interpolation turn the view over the next frames, whereas rotateToYaw snaps instantly. Use it for continuous follow-cameras where a snap would look jarring; the current yaw (getYaw) converges toward the target over several frames rather than changing at once.

Lua (x, y[, plane]) overloads

Every tile-taking camera function accepts raw coordinates in Lua — rotateToTile(tile), rotateToTile(x, y), or rotateToTile(x, y, plane) — and the same applies to mouseRotateToTile, keyboardRotateToTile, getYawForTile, getPitchForTile, and rotateToTileEvent. A script that didn't get a tile from an API like srs.player.position() can use the coordinate form directly, or build one with WorldTile.new(x, y[, plane]) (plain WorldTile(x, y) does not work).

docs.title: Ensure visible
docs.text:
Method Lua Ensure a tile is on-screen srs.camera.ensureVisible(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → bool Ensure an entity is on-screen srs.camera.ensureVisible(target) → bool

Opt-in helper to call before a canvas click: a no-op returning true when the target already projects to visible pixels, otherwise it rotates via rotateToTile / rotateToEntity. Returns false only when camera state can't be read or the rotation faults. A true does not guarantee same-frame projection — the engine renders one frame after the angle write, so the pixel lands on-screen next frame.

The Lua binding follows the same overload family as rotateToTile: ensureVisible(tile), ensureVisible(target), ensureVisible(x, y) (plane 0), or ensureVisible(x, y, plane).

docs.title: Mouse-rotation family
docs.text:
Method Lua Both axes srs.camera.mouseRotateTo(yaw, pitch) → bool Yaw only srs.camera.mouseRotateToYaw(yaw) → bool Pitch only srs.camera.mouseRotateToPitch(pitch) → bool Face a tile srs.camera.mouseRotateToTile(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → bool Face an entity srs.camera.mouseRotateToEntity(target) → bool

Same behaviour as the rotateTo* family. Falls back to the direct write path on this client — OSRS scroll-wheel is mapped to zoom, not rotation, and a true scroll-rotate isn't available without middle-mouse-drag support (TODO).

docs.title: Keyboard-rotation family
docs.text:
Method Lua Both axes srs.camera.keyboardRotateTo(yaw, pitch) → bool Yaw only srs.camera.keyboardRotateToYaw(yaw) → bool Pitch only srs.camera.keyboardRotateToPitch(pitch) → bool Face a tile srs.camera.keyboardRotateToTile(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → bool Face an entity srs.camera.keyboardRotateToEntity(target) → bool

Drives the game's arrow-key camera rotation. Slower, human-looking. The call queues the key hold and returns immediately; the camera finishes turning over the following frames.

docs.title: Zoom
docs.text:
Method Lua Set zoom level srs.camera.setZoom(zoom) → bool

setZoom injects mouse-wheel events into the game window until live zoom matches zoomLevel within tolerance. Returns false if the wheel injector or camera state isn't ready, or if zoom didn't converge after ~30 wheel ticks. The target is clamped to [getMinZoom(), getMaxZoom()]. This call blocks the script thread while it converges.

docs.title: Helper calculators (no side effects)
docs.text: Method Lua Yaw needed to face a tile srs.camera.getYawForTile(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → int Yaw needed to face an entity srs.camera.getYawForEntity(target) → int Pitch needed for a tile srs.camera.getPitchForTile(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → int Pitch needed for an entity srs.camera.getPitchForEntity(target) → int

docs.title: Low-level event firing
docs.text:
firePitchAndYawEvent clamps pitch and masks yaw like rotateTo. fireZoomEvent is not a direct write: it forwards to setZoom (blocking wheel injection, clamped to the zoom range) and returns nothing, so a failure to converge is silent — prefer setZoom and check its result.

Method Lua Raw pitch+yaw write (pitch first) srs.camera.firePitchAndYawEvent(pitch, yaw) Zoom (alias of setZoom, result discarded) srs.camera.fireZoomEvent(zoom)

docs.title: Event-based rotation (deferred execution)
docs.text:
A CameraEvent holds a pending rotation that the caller executes later. Stash one and run it on a different tick.

Method Lua Build "rotate to yaw/pitch" event srs.camera.rotateToEvent(yaw, pitch) → CameraEvent Yaw only srs.camera.rotateToYawEvent(yaw) → CameraEvent Pitch only srs.camera.rotateToPitchEvent(pitch) → CameraEvent Face a tile srs.camera.rotateToTileEvent(tile \| x, y[, plane]) → CameraEvent Face an entity srs.camera.rotateToEntityEvent(target) → CameraEvent Execute a stored event event:execute() → bool

CameraEvent fields:

Field Type Notes yaw integer -1 = leave this axis alone pitch integer -1 = leave this axis alone zoom integer -1 = leave this axis alone mode CameraMode Captured from getCameraMode() when built; informational only — execute always uses the direct write path

execute returns true if every set component succeeded; any negative axis counts as unset, and the call is a no-op if all axes are unset.

In Lua the usertype is CameraEvent and it is constructible: CameraEvent.new() gives an empty event (all axes -1) whose yaw, pitch, zoom, and mode fields are read/write — build one by hand instead of going through the factory functions:

local ev = CameraEvent.new()
ev.yaw = 1024
ev.zoom = 1500
script.onTick(function() ev:execute() end)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
local npc = entity.nearestNpc()
if npc then
    srs.camera.rotateToEntity(npc)
    srs.camera.setZoom(1500)
end

-- Or build a deferred event and execute next tick:
local pending = srs.camera.rotateToYawEvent(1024)
script.onTick(function() pending:execute() end)

docs.title: Cannon
docs.text:
srs.cannon

Dwarf Multicannon refill + repair.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Lua Refill nearest cannon srs.cannon.refill() → bool Repair nearest broken cannon srs.cannon.repair() → bool Has cannonball in inventory srs.cannon.hasCannonball() → bool

refill tries "Cannon base" first, then "Cannon" — the base's display name varies by setup stage. Returns false if no cannonball is held or no cannon is found.

repair tries a "Broken multicannon" first, then falls back to any nearby "Cannon" that offers a "Repair" option. Returns false if neither is found.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
Item ids (srs.cannon.*):

Lua const Value Item CANNONBALL 2 Cannonball GRANITE_CANNONBALL 17769 Granite cannonball

hasCannonball checks for any cannonball variant in the inventory.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
script.onTick(function()
    if srs.cannon.hasCannonball() then
        srs.cannon.refill()
    end
    srs.cannon.repair()  -- returns false unless a repairable cannon is nearby
end)

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
srs.chat

Read the game chatbox as an event stream. Every line the engine adds funnels through one native choke point, so a single subscription observes them all: server game / system messages (the minigame and boss status lines), public player chat, private messages, clan / friends-chat, broadcasts, and the friend login/out notifier. There is no polling reader — chat is delivered only as events.

System vs. player messages

sender is empty for server/system (game) messages and non-empty for player chat. That is the robust way to tell a minigame/boss status line from someone actually talking — prefer it over matching on type, since server game messages are server-driven and don't carry one fixed type value.

Callback thread

The callback is delivered on the script thread (queued by the hook, drained once per frame), so it is safe to call the rest of the srs.* API from it. Per-script pause applies.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Lua Subscribe to chat lines srs.chat.onMessage(fn) → token Unsubscribe srs.chat.offMessage(token) → bool

onMessage fires for every line, not just messages aimed at you — filter in your handler. Returns a token; pass it to offMessage to stop listening.

fn receives a table {type, sender, message, channel, wallClock} (see Types).

Unsubscribing

srs.chat.offMessage(token) removes the callback registered under that token. It is safe to call from inside the callback itself. Returns false for an unknown or already-removed token. A full script reload clears all subscriptions automatically, so a register-once-at-load callback needs no explicit cleanup.

docs.title: Chat types
docs.text:
srs.chat.type.* — engine chat-type ints to compare against event.type. GAMEMESSAGE and PUBLIC are the two you can rely on; treat the rest as best-effort labels. Server / system messages do not use a single value — level-ups and examines arrive as GAMEMESSAGE (0), while filterable "spam" like eating or skilling comes through as 105, and broadcasts use others still. So the robust "is this a system line?" test is an empty sender (player chat always has a sender), not a type match. Log event.type to discover others on your build.

Constant Value Meaning GAMEMESSAGE 0 Server / system message — level-ups, examine (verified) PUBLIC 2 Local player public chat (verified) PRIVATE_IN 3 Private message received LOGIN_LOGOUT 5 "X has logged in/out." (friend notifier) MOD_PRIVATE 6 Private message from a Jagex mod PRIVATE_OUT 7 Private message you sent FRIENDS_CHAT 9 Friends-chat channel message CLAN_CHAT 41 Clan chat (unverified on this build) CLAN_GUEST_CHAT 42 Guest clan chat (unverified on this build) CONSOLE 99 In-game console / client widget log

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
ChatMessageEvent (the table passed to the onMessage callback):

Field Type Notes type integer Engine chat-type int (see Chat types) sender string Empty for server/system (game) messages message string The visible line body channel string Clan / friends-chat name (empty for most) wallClock number Millisecond timestamp (system tick count) when the message was observed

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
local myName = srs.player.displayName()

srs.chat.onMessage(function(e)
    -- 1) Minigame / boss status: server messages have an EMPTY sender
    if e.sender == "" then
        if e.message:find("wave") or e.message:find("enrage") then
            log.info("STATUS: " .. e.message)
        end
        return
    end

    -- 2) Someone talking to us by name (public chat has a sender)
    if myName and e.message:lower():find(myName:lower(), 1, true) then
        log.info(e.sender .. " mentioned us: " .. e.message)
    end
end)

docs.title: Combat
docs.text:
srs.combat

Combat-tab queries and toggles. Reads come from the player's varps; writes click widgets on the combat tab (group 593). setAutoRetaliate is a no-op if already in the desired state; toggleSpec and setAttackStyle always click.

Combat tab must be open

setAttackStyle and setAutoRetaliate click combat-tab widgets, so when a click is needed they return false unless the combat tab is the open sidebar tab — open it first from your script. toggleSpec is the exception (see below).

Backed by these varps:

Varp Meaning 300 Special-attack energy (0..1000, 100% = 1000) 301 Special-attack enabled flag (0/1) 172 Auto-retaliate (0 = on, 1 = off, inverted)

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Lua Spec energy (0..1000) srs.combat.specEnergy() → integer Spec energy (0..100 %) srs.combat.specEnergyPct() → integer Spec enabled flag srs.combat.isSpecEnabled() → bool Currently in combat srs.combat.isInCombat() → bool Interacting with anything srs.combat.isInteracting() → bool Engaged with this target srs.combat.isInteractingWith(target) → bool The NPC we're interacting with srs.combat.interactingWith() → ActionTarget \| nil Raw interact target (kind + index) srs.combat.interactTarget() → table \| nil Auto-retaliate on srs.combat.isAutoRetaliate() → bool Toggle special attack srs.combat.toggleSpec() → bool Set attack style srs.combat.setAttackStyle(style) → bool Set auto-retaliate srs.combat.setAutoRetaliate(on) → bool

Auto-retaliate sense

The underlying varp is inverted (0 = on, 1 = off); isAutoRetaliate / setAutoRetaliate expose the natural sense (true = retaliate is on).

toggleSpec clicks the minimap special-attack orb (group 160), which is rendered whatever sidebar tab is open, and only falls back to the combat-tab button when the orb isn't drawn — so scripts never have to switch tabs first. Its true return means the click was dispatched, not that the special attack was used: confirm on a later tick. Combat weapons set the enabled flag (isSpecEnabled) until the next hit; instant specials such as the woodcutting axes' Lumber Up never set it, and the proof is the energy (specEnergyPct) dropping below 100.

-- Fire an axe spec and confirm it landed.
local before = srs.combat.specEnergyPct()
if before >= 100 and srs.combat.toggleSpec() then
    script.nextTick(function()
        if srs.combat.specEnergyPct() < before then log.info("spec used") end
    end)
end

docs.title: Interact target
docs.text:
The local player's target is stored as a kind (NPC / player / world entity) plus an index within that kind. For NPCs and players that index is the server spawn index — the same number as ActionTarget.spawnIndex — so it compares directly against a target you already hold.

Never read the index on its own

Dropping a target clears the kind but leaves the last index behind, so a bare index != -1 latches as a permanent "still engaged". Every call on this page applies the kind check for you — always go through them rather than testing interactTarget().index yourself.

  • isInteracting() — true while we are interacting with anything. Because it reads only our own action, it stays correct in multi-combat where other players fighting the same NPC would confuse a scan.
  • isInteractingWith(target) — exact: matches the engine's index against that target's spawnIndex under a matching kind. False for the neighbouring NPC of the same id, and false the moment the game retargets us or the target dies. The Lua form takes an ActionTarget from any entity/npc finder.
  • interactingWith() — returns the NPC itself, resolved against the live NPC list, or nil. Prefer this over the predicate when the script needs to see a retarget (a boss swapping to a clone, an aggressive mob pulling us off the intended kill) rather than only learning that its own target stopped matching. nil when idle, when the target is a player / world entity, or when it despawned this tick.
  • interactTarget() — the raw read, no scene lookup. Survives the target leaving the NPC list, and is the only one that also reports player targets (following / attacking in PvP). It returns a fixed-shape table { kind = "npc"|"player"|"worldEntity", kindId = 1|2|3, index = <spawnIndex> }, or nil when not interacting.

Indices are recycled

An index is unique only per kind, and is reused when an NPC respawns. Pass a target from the current tick's query, not one cached across a despawn.

isInCombat is the broader question: true when we are interacting with something or some NPC is interacting with us. Use it for "am I in a fight at all"; use isInteractingWith / interactingWith for "am I on the right target".

Ground truth for 'am I actually attacking'

The interact target says what the client intends. For what actually landed — damage dealt, damage taken, whether a prayer blocked it — read srs.hitsplats instead.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
AttackStyle (srs.combat.*):

Lua const Value FIRST 0 SECOND 1 THIRD 2 FOURTH 3

Indexes the 4-button style row on the combat tab; meaning varies by weapon (e.g. for scimitar: Chop / Slash / Lunge / Block).

Interact kind (the kind string plus numeric kindId in the interactTarget() table):

kindId kind string Notes 0 — (nil returned) Not interacting 1 "npc" index = NPC spawn index 2 "player" index = player index 3 "worldEntity" Boats / player-owned instances; not resolvable via the NPC or player list

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
script.onTick(function()
    srs.combat.setAutoRetaliate(true)
    if srs.combat.specEnergyPct() >= 50
            and not srs.combat.isSpecEnabled() then
        srs.combat.toggleSpec()
    end
    if not srs.combat.isInCombat() then
        log.info("idle — find a new target")
    end
end)

docs.title: Detecting a retarget
docs.text:
local myTarget   -- the NPC we chose to fight

script.onTick(function()
    if myTarget and not srs.combat.isInteractingWith(myTarget) then
        local actual = srs.combat.interactingWith()
        if actual then
            log.warn("pulled onto " .. actual.name .. " — re-attacking ours")
            myTarget:attack()
        elseif not srs.combat.isInteracting() then
            myTarget = nil          -- target died / we went idle
        end
    end
end)

docs.title: Defs
docs.text:
srs.defs

Read-only definition / cache metadata — "what is this thing" (static per-id data decoded from the game's type structs), as opposed to the live-entity finders (srs.npc, srs.gameobject) that give you a specific on-screen instance's position / animation / HP. It covers the definition fields the client actually decodes.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Lua NPC definition from a live target or an id srs.defs.npc(target \| id) → table Item definition by id srs.defs.item(id) → table

docs.title: srs.defs.npc(target | id)
docs.text:
Resolve an NPC's definition metadata — size (tile footprint), maxHp, and the full actions list — that the finders don't carry on the entry. Pass either a live target from srs.npc.* / entity.*, or a raw NPC id. Returns a table:

Field Type Notes id integer NPC definition id name string Display name size integer Tile-footprint side maxHp integer actions table of strings Non-empty right-click options, in slot order valid boolean false if the definition couldn't be read (e.g. the NPC despawned — then only id / name / maxHp are filled in)

Target vs id

  • srs.defs.npc(target) reads the live NPC currently in the scene — instant.
  • srs.defs.npc(id) resolves the definition straight from the game's cache, so it works for any id, including NPCs not on screen. It loads-on-miss, marshalled to the engine thread, so it can block up to ~3 s the first time an off-scene id is requested (instant once decoded) — call it from pulse / onTick, never draw, and prefer the target form when you already have a live NPC.

Combat level is not part of this table — read .combatLevel from the srs.npc.* / entity.* entry instead (-1 when the NPC shows no level).

-- by a live target (instant)
local n = srs.npc.nearest()
if n then local d = srs.defs.npc(n); log.info(d.name .. " maxHp=" .. d.maxHp) end

-- by raw id (works off-screen; may block briefly on first lookup)
local zulrah = srs.defs.npc(2042)
if zulrah.valid then log.info(zulrah.name .. " size=" .. zulrah.size) end

local n = srs.npc.nearest()
if n then
    local def = srs.defs.npc(n)
    if def.valid then
        log.info(def.name .. "  size=" .. def.size .. "  maxHp=" .. def.maxHp)
        for _, a in ipairs(def.actions) do
            log.info("  action: " .. a)   -- e.g. "Attack", "Talk-to", "Pickpocket"
        end
    end
end

docs.title: srs.defs.item(id)
docs.text:
Resolve an item's full definition metadata by id. Works for any id, including off-screen items the renderer never touches. Returns a table:

Field Type Notes id integer The item id you passed name string In-game display name (e.g. "Prayer potion(4)") examine string Examine text stackable boolean Stacks into one inventory slot tradeable boolean GE-tradeable equipable boolean Has an equipment slot equipSlot integer Equipment slot index; -1 if not equipable value integer Shop/GE base value (high alch ≈ value * 0.6) weight integer Engine weight units notedId integer Noted↔unnoted linked id (the "cert" id) placeholderId integer Bank placeholder linked id valid boolean false only when the id can't be resolved at all

May block briefly on a cache miss

Resolution uses the same path as srs.game.itemName: a live item-cache read (instant) when the id is already decoded — inventory, bank, equipment, hovered ground — otherwise a load-on-demand decode marshalled to the engine thread that blocks up to ~3 s. Call it from pulse / onTick, never from draw. For hot loops over known ids, resolve once and cache the table.

local def = srs.defs.item(12791)          -- Rune pouch
if def.valid then
    log.info(def.name .. " — " .. def.examine)
    log.info("stackable=" .. tostring(def.stackable) ..
             "  tradeable=" .. tostring(def.tradeable) ..
             "  alch≈" .. math.floor(def.value * 0.6))
end

Loc definitions

Loc/object definitions are handled at the source rather than via a separate srs.defs.loc: the object lookup resolves the multiloc transform, so a _PARENT loc (GOTR portals, staged doors/banks) reports its varbit-selected child's real name + actions through the existing object.lookup / GameObjectEntry.actions / hasAction / byName / interactFirstAvailable surfaces instead of coming back empty.

docs.title: DepositBox
docs.text:
srs.depositbox

Deposit-box variant of bank operations. Reads the player's inventory (container 93) directly — there's no separate "deposit-box container". Group 192 (BankDepositbox) hosts the buttons and the deposit-side item grid (child 24).

Same pattern as Bank: open (via the scene loc), close, bulk- deposit buttons, per-item depositAllExcept, and the quantity preset.

docs.title: State
docs.text: Method Lua Is deposit box open srs.depositbox.isOpen() → bool

docs.title: Open / close
docs.text:
Method Lua Open via nearest loc srs.depositbox.open() → bool Close (X-button) srs.depositbox.close() → bool

open mirrors srs.bank.open's nearest-object resolution but targets a scene loc instead of a banker NPC: it tries "Bank deposit box" then "Deposit box", resolves the nearest instance that actually exposes the "Deposit" verb (decorative twins are filtered), cancels any in-flight walk, and fires OPLOC1 on the loc's SW anchor. Returns true if the box is already open (no-op) or the click was issued — it does not mean the interface is open yet, so check isOpen() on a later tick. Returns false if no deposit box is in scene.

close clicks the title-bar close "X" (a runtime-created child of component (192, 1)) — the same shape as the bank's own close. Returns false if the box isn't open or the button isn't rendered this frame.

docs.title: Bulk deposit
docs.text: Method Lua Deposit whole inventory srs.depositbox.depositInventory() → bool Deposit worn equipment srs.depositbox.depositEquipment() → bool Deposit looting bag srs.depositbox.depositLootingBag() → bool

docs.title: Per-item deposit
docs.text:
The deposit-side inventory is widget (192, 24) — the box renders the player's backpack in its own grid (not the sidebar). Each deposit is a widget click on that grid cell (backpack slot 0..27) using the item's first op (op index 1).

Method Lua Deposit all except (by id) srs.depositbox.depositAllExcept({ids...}) → bool Deposit all except (by name) srs.depositbox.depositAllExcept({"names"...}) → bool

depositAllExcept fires one deposit click on the FIRST non-kept inventory slot per call and returns false; the script polls each tick until only kept items remain, at which point it returns true (it also returns false if the box isn't open). The by-name form matches by case-insensitive substring of the item's name ("pickaxe" keeps every pickaxe); the by-id form matches exactly.

docs.title: The item ops are positional
docs.text:
The box's item ops are positional: op index 1 is whichever quantity the quantity preset currently selects — not literally Deposit-All — and the action string passed along with the click is cosmetic, since only the index dispatches. A click labelled "Deposit-All" therefore deposits a single item while the preset says 1, which is what the box opens on.

depositAllExcept handles this for you: before its first deposit click it reads the preset and, if it isn't ALL, clicks the All button and returns false. The next poll deposits normally — one extra tick per box visit, no blocking, and scripts never need to touch the preset themselves. A pack that is entirely kept items still returns true immediately without changing the preset.

Op index not yet re-verified on the current client

The positional "op 1 = preset quantity" mapping was measured before the 241.1 client update; the bank's deposit ops were re-read and renumbered in that update. If depositAllExcept deposits the wrong amount, re-check the box's menu before blaming the preset logic.

If you fire the ops yourself rather than through depositAllExcept, select ALL first and check it landed with getQuantity — do not assume the op that worked under one preset means the same thing under another.

Keeping an in-inventory tool (e.g. a pickaxe) is the primary use case:

-- Bank ore at the deposit box while keeping the pickaxe in the pack.
if srs.depositbox.open() and srs.depositbox.isOpen() then
  if srs.depositbox.depositAllExcept({ "Bronze pickaxe", "Gem bag" }) then
    srs.depositbox.close()
  end
end

docs.title: Quantity preset
docs.text:
Method Lua Set quantity srs.depositbox.setQuantity(q) → bool Read quantity srs.depositbox.getQuantity() → q \| nil

Quantity constants (srs.depositbox.*): ONE, FIVE, TEN, X, ALL. Same set as Bank; the Shop Quantity enum differs — ONE / FIVE / TEN / FIFTY / X, no ALL — so don't reuse constants across the tables.

setQuantity clicks the matching 1/5/10/X/All button and needs the box open. getQuantity reads varbit DEPOSITBOX_MODE (4430) instead, so it works whether or not the box is open — the preset is sticky across visits. It returns nil if the varbit can't be read. Use it rather than reading 4430 yourself: the raw values are not in button order (measured in-client 2026-07-14 — 1=0, 5=1, All=2, X=3, 10=4), so the mapping is not something to infer from the button layout.

-- The preset is sticky, so a script that fires the item ops directly
-- should confirm it rather than trust the box's default.
if srs.depositbox.getQuantity() ~= srs.depositbox.ALL then
  srs.depositbox.setQuantity(srs.depositbox.ALL)
  return  -- re-poll next tick; the click needs a tick to land
end

docs.title: Dialogue
docs.text:
srs.dialogue

Detect and advance OSRS dialogue. Continue prompts use the spacebar (the game's built-in keybind); option menus use number keys 1..9. Option 10+ requires a mouse click on the option row (not implemented here).

docs.title: ⚠️ A Messagebox is not a blocking gate
docs.text:
isOpen() does not mean "the game is waiting on you."

Widget group 229 (Messagebox) is an informational chatbox notice — e.g. "Your inventory is too full to hold any more pay-dirt." with a "Click here to continue" line. Unlike NPC chat it does not pause the game: your character keeps walking, mining and clicking while it's up, and almost any action (walking especially) clears it on its own.

So this idiom — which earlier versions of this page recommended — wedges your script forever the moment a Messagebox appears:

-- ❌ BROKEN: spins forever on a Messagebox.
if srs.dialogue.isOpen() then
    if srs.dialogue.hasContinue() then srs.dialogue.clickContinue() end
    return   -- nothing else ever runs
end

It fails silently and is nasty to diagnose: the state machine keeps reporting its intended state while the executor never runs, so every log line looks healthy. Gate blocking work on isOpen() and not isMessagebox() instead — see the example below.

hasContinue() is true for a Messagebox, and correctly so: 229 really does own a continue component (229.4 Messagebox.CONTINUE). It answers "does this dialogue have a continue arrow", not "is the game blocked". Use isMessagebox() to tell informational, ignore it from must advance.

docs.title: ⚠️ The text prompt is blocking, and isOpen() does not see it
docs.text:
The chatbox text / amount prompt — "Enter amount:", "Enter name:", "How many?", a password door — is the mirror-image trap. It renders in the chatbox (group 162, Chatbox.MES_TEXT 162.43 / MES_TEXT2 162.44), not in any dialogue group, so isOpen(), hasContinue() and hasOptions() are all false while it is up — yet the game is waiting on typed input, and Space, number keys and clicks on the world do nothing useful until it is answered or dismissed.

A runner that gates only on isOpen() will happily run its state machine into a prompt it cannot see. Test isTextPrompt() as a blocking state of its own, right next to the dialogue gate, and answer it with enterText / enterAmount (or dismiss it with srs.input.pressEscape()):

if srs.dialogue.isTextPrompt() then
    srs.dialogue.enterAmount(101)     -- blocks: waits, types, Enter
    return                            -- blocking: nothing else this tick
elseif srs.dialogue.isOpen() and not srs.dialogue.isMessagebox() then
    -- continue / option handling as below
    return
end

docs.title: Widget groups
docs.text:
Widget groups, and which are advanceable with clickContinue:

Group Kind Blocks game? Advance with 229 Messagebox — plain text No — informational clickContinue (or just ignore it) 217 ChatRight — player dialogue (head on right) Yes clickContinue 231 ChatLeft — NPC dialogue (head on left) Yes clickContinue 60 ChatBoth — two-portrait Yes clickContinue 193 Objectbox — single-sprite Yes clickContinue (keystroke only) 11 ObjectboxDouble — two-sprite Yes clickContinue 219 Chatmenu — "Select an Option" menu Yes selectOption / selectOptionByText

Every group except 219 is a continue-style dialog, and hasContinue() is true for all of them. 219 is the only one that needs selectOption.

docs.title: Mechanism, and what clickContinue's return value means
docs.text:
clickContinue and selectOption post a real key press (press, char and release, exactly as a physical key would produce). They are fire-and-forget: they enqueue the keystroke and return immediately.

true means "keystroke dispatched", not "dialogue advanced." Never treat the return value as confirmation. Poll isOpen() / hasContinue() on a later tick to see whether it landed, and give the dialogue a tick or two — a dialogue that is still up on the very next tick has not necessarily failed.

If a live test shows the keystroke doesn't take for some group, clickContinueByClick() does the same job with a real mouse click on the group's continue component. It blocks the calling script (mouse move + click drain), so keep clickContinue as the per-tick default and reach for the click only as a fallback.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text: Method Lua Any dialogue open srs.dialogue.isOpen() → bool Continue-style dialog up srs.dialogue.hasContinue() → bool Informational message (229) up srs.dialogue.isMessagebox() → bool Option-select up srs.dialogue.hasOptions() → bool Advance continue (keystroke, non-blocking) srs.dialogue.clickContinue() → bool Advance continue (mouse fallback, blocks) srs.dialogue.clickContinueByClick() → bool Pick option (1-based) srs.dialogue.selectOption(n) → bool List option labels (never includes the menu's title row — "Select an Option" or a custom question — so options()[i] is exactly what selectOption(i) presses) srs.dialogue.options() → table Pick by label (exact match first, then substring) srs.dialogue.selectOptionByText(text) → bool Current dialogue body text srs.dialogue.getDialogueText() → string Body contains substring srs.dialogue.hasDialogueText(sub) → bool Any option contains substring srs.dialogue.hasDialogueOption(sub) → bool

docs.title: Chatbox text / amount prompt
docs.text:
Method Lua Text / amount prompt up srs.dialogue.isTextPrompt() → bool Wait for it, type text, Enter (blocks) srs.dialogue.enterText(text[, timeoutMs]) → bool Wait for it, type a number, Enter (blocks) srs.dialogue.enterAmount(n[, timeoutMs]) → bool

isTextPrompt() is true while either prompt child (162.43 / 162.44) is rendered — the "Enter amount:" integer prompt and the string prompts share the widget. enterText / enterAmount poll for the prompt first (default timeoutMs 2400 — the prompt is server-driven, so it lands a tick plus round-trip after whatever triggered it), type the value with human pacing (80–160 ms between characters, through the engine's input-event queue — see Input), then tap Enter. They block the calling script for the whole sequence, so call them from pulse / onTick, never from draw, and once per prompt rather than every tick. false means the prompt never opened (nothing is typed then); true means typed and submitted, not accepted — poll isTextPrompt() a tick later if you need to know it closed. These are the same calls as srs.prompt.*, placed here so dialogue-driven code has them next to the queries it already polls.

selectOptionByText tries a case-insensitive exact match first, then a case-insensitive substring match; hasDialogueText and hasDialogueOption use case-insensitive substring matching. getDialogueText returns the body text of the open dialog (empty if none is up or it hasn't populated yet); hasDialogueText / hasDialogueOption are pure queries — they don't click.

docs.title: Aliases
docs.text:
Convenience names — each is a thin wrapper:

Method Lua Same as isOpen srs.dialogue.isInDialogue() → bool Same as hasOptions srs.dialogue.hasSelectAnOption() → bool Same as clickContinue srs.dialogue.continueSpace() → bool Same as selectOption(n) / selectOptionByText(text) srs.dialogue.clickOption(n \| text) → bool

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Advance real dialogue, but never let an informational message stop the script working. The rule: only a non-Messagebox dialogue earns a return.

-- A Messagebox blocks nothing — nudge it and carry on working.
if srs.dialogue.isMessagebox() then
    srs.dialogue.clickContinue()
    -- deliberately no return — walking clears it anyway
elseif srs.dialogue.hasOptions() then
    srs.dialogue.selectOptionByText("Yes")
    return                        -- real dialogue: game is blocked
elseif srs.dialogue.hasContinue() then
    srs.dialogue.clickContinue()
    return                        -- real dialogue: game is blocked
end

Because clickContinue reports dispatch rather than success, a script that must not stall on an unexpected dialogue should also cap how long it will keep trying — count consecutive ticks a dialogue has been open and fall through past a small budget, rather than returning forever.

docs.title: Drawing
docs.text:
srs.draw

Overlay drawing.

For a themed, batteries-included HUD (dark-glass panels, per-skill accents, XP rows, animated bars, level rings) layered on top of these primitives, see Overlay (srs.overlay).

script.draw only

Only valid inside a script.draw(fn) callback. The host guarantees a live in-game ImGui frame there; calling from pulse / onTick will fault on builds where those paths run off-frame.

Coordinates are game-canvas pixels

All positions and sizes here (widgetRect, anchorToWidget, beginOverlay, the foreground draw list, overlaySize) are in game canvas pixels — the same space as widget rects and world-to-screen projection. When the game's UI scaling is compensated, the host maps them onto the window for you, scaling thickness, radius, rounding and text size as well; scripts never convert.

docs.title: Anchoring
docs.text:
Pin overlays to OSRS widgets so they follow tab switches and layout mode changes.

Method Lua Live widget rect (cached) srs.draw.widgetRect(g, c) → Rect \| nil Compute pinned screen position srs.draw.anchorToWidget(g, c, corner, dx?, dy?, pivot?) → Vec2 \| nil Evict cached rects srs.draw.clearAnchorCache()

Anchor miss policy

anchorToWidget / widgetRect return the last seen rect for that (group, child) pair when the widget isn't drawn this frame. This keeps overlays pinned through brief widget flicker (tab switches, loading frames). Call clearAnchorCache() on logout or layout mode change to evict.

docs.title: Window lifecycle
docs.text:
Method Lua Open overlay at pos (canvas px) srs.draw.beginOverlay(name, pos, pivot?, bgAlpha?) → bool One-call: anchor + begin srs.draw.beginAnchoredOverlay(name, g, c, corner, dx?, dy?, pivot?, bgAlpha?) → bool Close overlay srs.draw.endOverlay() Inner size of the open overlay srs.draw.overlaySize() → Vec2

When the game's UI scaling is compensated, an overlay's content (font, padding, explicit widget sizes) is scaled by the same factor as the game UI.

overlaySize() returns the inner (padding-excluded) size of the innermost open overlay window, in canvas pixels. Call it between begin* and endOverlay. An auto-resizing window reports last frame's layout, so you can fit custom art (drawLine / drawFilledRect behind a dummy()) to the panel your text rows actually produced. Returns {0, 0} outside any window.

Pair every begin* that returns true with one endOverlay. beginAnchoredOverlay returns false when the widget has never been seen (no cached rect either); in that case do NOT call endOverlay.

local changed, v = srs.draw.checkbox("Enable", v)
if changed then onToggle(v) end

    if srs.draw.beginAnchoredOverlay(
            "##my-overlay", 162, 0,
            srs.Corner.TopLeft, 0, -4) then
        srs.draw.textColored(srs.colors.Orange, "Barbarian Fishing")
        srs.draw.separator()
        srs.draw.text("Mode: Drop fish")

        srs.draw.endOverlay()
    end
end)

docs.title: Engine
docs.text:
srs.engine

Engine-level introspection and low-level primitives. Two distinct surfaces live in the same Lua table:

  1. Action-cap introspection — observe the per-server-tick action counter the client maintains and resets every game tick.
  2. Diagnostic primitives — low-level helpers (VarClient reads / writes, raw CS2 runScript, input-block toggle) intended for one-shot diagnostic probes, not production scripts.

Scripts MUST NOT block

Script callbacks (pulse / onTick / nextTick) run on the script worker thread; a blocked callback stalls your script. To gate on action capacity, check canDispatchAction() and yield via script.nextTick(...) if it returns false — never spin-wait.

docs.title: Action-cap introspection
docs.text:
The OSRS server enforces a cap of 8 action-class packets per game cycle (vanilla). The client counts every action-class packet — object, NPC, ground-item and widget-button actions, etc. — but not input traffic (mouse moves, clicks, key events, heartbeats). Note that a sidebar tab switch counts: a chrome-tab click emits IF_BUTTON like any other widget click.

The client's action dispatcher has a budget gate, but it defers an over-cap action rather than dropping it — it fires some unbounded number of ticks later, against a world that has moved on. That is fine for a drop-all and wrong for anything tick-scoped.

These accessors are raw observations, not a safety net. If you need several actions inside one tick, and need to know which ones the tick could not afford, use srs.actions.batch: it paces the ladder at the engine's one-action-per-frame floor, fails fast on the cap instead of deferring, and reports every step per outcome.

Method Lua Actions sent this tick srs.engine.actionsSentThisTick() → int Per-tick action cap srs.engine.actionLimit() → int Can dispatch another? srs.engine.canDispatchAction() → bool Lifetime action count srs.engine.totalActionsCounted() → number

canDispatchAction() is a probabilistic guard, not a guarantee — the server has the final say, and the client observes what it sent, not what the server processed. For burst-action scripts the match is much closer to engine behaviour than a blind sleep.

actionLimit() is currently the constant 8. If a future OSRS revision makes the cap per-opcode, the method signature will keep returning a single int and an opcode-aware overload will be added alongside.

script.onTick(function()
  if srs.engine.canDispatchAction() then
    srs.inventory.dropAll("Big bones")
  end
end)

docs.title: Diagnostic primitives (Lua-only)
docs.text: For one-shot diagnostic probes and scripts that need a CS2 hook the high-level API doesn't expose yet.

docs.title: VarClient + CS2
docs.text:
Method Lua Read a VarClientInt; nil if the id is unset srs.engine.getVarcInt(varcId) → int or nil Write a VarClientInt srs.engine.setVarcInt(varcId, value) → bool Invoke a CS2 client script (variadic ints only; false if it can't run) srs.engine.runScript(scriptId, ...args) → bool

runScript powers things like the bank scrollbar sync (runScript(UPDATE_SCROLLBAR, ...)); use it when there's no purpose-built API for the CS2 routine you need to drive.

-- Read the current bank scroll position (VarClientInt BANK_SCROLL = 51)
local scrollY = srs.engine.getVarcInt(51)

docs.title: Input-block toggle
docs.text:
The script engine holds an input gate that prevents the user's clicks from racing the script's spoofed clicks (which would corrupt the engine's click slot mid-spoof). These two calls pop / push that gate.

Method Lua Lift the gate so the user can interact with the game mid-script srs.engine.releaseInputBlock() Restore the gate srs.engine.takeInputBlock()

Production scripts MUST NOT call these

Leaving user input enabled mid-spoof corrupts the engine's click slot. Use this only where you are testing something locally and want to see what value would be returned by a manual action on the client. The gate is re-taken automatically on script reload.

docs.text:
• Inventory — pendingDropCount() works hand-in-hand with canDispatchAction() for paced drop loops.
  • Bank — already documents the same srs.engine.* diagnostic helpers under its "Engineering primitives" section.

docs.title: Entity
docs.text:
entity.* (global table)

Live query over NPCs and players in the loaded scene. Returns ActionTarget values you can pass into srs.npc or call action shortcuts on directly (:attack(), :talkTo()).

Global table

Lives at Lua global scope, not under srs.* — entity.npcs(), not srs.entity.npcs(). Kept this way for source-compat with earlier scripts.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Lua Returns All NPCs in scene entity.npcs() ActionTarget[] All players in scene entity.players() ActionTarget[] Both entity.all() ActionTarget[] Closest NPC (Chebyshev) entity.nearestNpc() ActionTarget \| nil Closest player entity.nearestPlayer() ActionTarget \| nil Players within radius entity.playersWithin(x, y, radius [, plane]) ActionTarget[] NPCs within radius entity.npcsWithin(x, y, radius [, plane]) ActionTarget[] NPCs by NpcType id entity.npcById(id) ActionTarget[] NPCs by name entity.npcByName(name) ActionTarget[]

Name lookups are case- and whitespace-insensitive. Empty result if the cache hasn't decoded a matching NpcType yet (rare).

Global npc.* finder aliases

The global npc table (npc.all(), npc.byId(id), npc.byName(name), npc.nearest(), npc.nearestById(id), npc.nearestByName(name)) aliases the same EntityQuery backend and also returns ActionTargets. The finder surface is documented once on Npc — prefer that page for the full table.

docs.title: Radius queries
docs.text:
entity.playersWithin(x, y, radius) returns the players whose tile is within radius tiles of (x, y) measured as Chebyshev distance (max(|dx|, |dy|) — a square ring, the same metric the game uses for NPC aggression). Pass an optional 4th plane argument to restrict to a single plane; omit it for any plane. entity.npcsWithin(...) is the NPC companion — but note that visible NPC planes are currently normalized to 0, so the plane filter is effectively any-plane for NPCs (omit it).

This is the built-in form of a "count nearby players" anti-crash scan (every player within r tiles of t):

-- Number of OTHER players within 2 tiles of a vein
local crowd = #entity.playersWithin(vein.tileX, vein.tileY, 2)

Self-inclusion

entity.players(), entity.nearestPlayer(), and entity.playersWithin() never include the local player — the local render slot is skipped when the list is built. You do not need to hand-filter your own tile / name out of the results. If you ever need your own position, use srs.player.* (e.g. srs.player.displayName() / the player-position API), not the entity list.

docs.title: ActionTarget
docs.text:
Read-only fields:

Field Type Notes kind integer See TargetKind table below tileX / tileY / tileZ integer World tile coords plane integer 0–3 spawnIndex integer Server slot (NPC) or render slot (Player) entityId integer NpcType id / item id / LocType id by kind name string Display name currentHp integer Current HP — -1 when no head-bar is visible (server pushes ratio for ~6 s after a hit, then it goes unknowable) maxHp integer Inferred from health-bar ratio + NpcType interactTarget integer Index of the actor this target is interacting with, within the kind given by interactTargetKind (-1 if none) interactTargetKind integer 0 none, 1 NPC (interactTarget = NPC spawnIndex), 2 player (= player spawnIndex), 3 world entity. Always check it before comparing interactTarget animationId integer Active anim id (-1 if idle) modelMagnitude integer Engine getXYZMag half-extent of the model (0 = unknown) overheadText string Overhead chat text drawn above the actor right now ("" = none). NPC forced chat and player public chat alike; the engine clears it when its countdown expires. Snapshot at query time — srs.npc.overheadText(target) re-reads live overheadCycles integer Client ticks left before overheadText clears (0 = none) orientation integer Facing angle, 0–2047, clockwise from south: 0 = S, 512 = W, 1024 = N, 1536 = E; -1 = unknown. NPCs and players. This is the actor's target facing — the rendered model catches up within a few ticks combatLevel integer Combat level; -1 = unknown. NPCs and players. NPCs that show no level on the right-click (bankers, pets) read -1

TargetKind values (also available as the Lua global enum TargetKind, e.g. TargetKind.Npc):

Value Kind 0 None (unset) 1 Npc 2 Player 3 Object (Loc) 4 Tile

Methods:

Method Lua What it does Still in scene? target:isValid() → bool kind != None Still alive? target:isAlive() → bool Despawn check (NPCs) Generic action target:interact(action) → bool Same path as srs.npc.interact; action is any menu-option string Attack shortcut target:attack() → bool Talk shortcut target:talkTo() → bool Banker shortcut target:bank() → bool "Bank" action Overhead prayer target:overheadPrayer() → OverheadPrayer Protection-prayer headicon the NPC is showing (e.g. boss phases); returns the global OverheadPrayer enum (None / Melee / Missiles / Magic / Retribution / Smite / Redemption) Spot animations target:spotAnims() → table Array of {slot, id, height, startCycle, delay, active} for the graphics playing on the actor now (empty table when none). Details on Npc Has a spot animation target:hasSpotAnim(id) → bool

All action methods are fail-closed via the always-on spoofer — see the Npc page for the full contract.

There is no target:examine() method on the usertype — use srs.npc.examine(target) instead.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
-- Attack the nearest cow
local cow = entity.npcByName("Cow")[1]
if cow and cow:isAlive() then
    cow:attack()
end

-- Combat-style retaliation gate: is any nearby NPC fighting me?
local me = srs.player.displayName()
for _, npc in ipairs(entity.npcs()) do
    local opp = npc.interactTarget
    if npc.interactTargetKind == 2 then   -- 2 = targeting a player
        local players = entity.players()
        for _, p in ipairs(players) do
            if p.spawnIndex == opp and p.name == me then
                log.info("Being attacked by " .. npc.name)
                break
            end
        end
    end
end

docs.title: Equipment
docs.text:
srs.equipment

Worn-items view plus equip/unequip actions. Slot indices follow the game's equipment slot numbering (gaps are intentional; see the constants below).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Lua All worn items srs.equipment.all() → table Specific slot srs.equipment.at(slot) → EquippedItem \| nil Wearing item id srs.equipment.isWearing(id) → boolean Wearing item name srs.equipment.isWearing(name) → boolean Equip from backpack srs.equipment.equip(id \| name) → boolean Unequip a slot srs.equipment.unequip(slot) → boolean

Name lookups match the item's in-game display name (case- and whitespace-insensitive substring).

all returns only equipped items — empty slots are filtered out.

equip resolves the item's own equip verb from its ItemType — you don't pass "Wield" vs "Wear"; it reads the item's action list and clicks whichever of Wield / Wear / Equip / Hold applies. unequip fires "Remove" on the Worn Equipment interface, opening the equipment tab if needed.

Runtime-verify

unequip uses the slot's standard primary op. If it no-ops in-game for a particular slot, fall back to clicking the item through srs.widget.click.

equip returns false when the item isn't in the backpack; if the item's equip verb can't be read it falls back to "Wear".

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
srs.events (Lua)

A central registry for engine events. Subscribe a callback to a named event and it fires once per occurrence, delivered on the script thread with a single payload table. This is the general-purpose counterpart to the dedicated srs.chat.onMessage / srs.projectiles.onSpawned streams — one on(name, fn) entry point for the rest of the engine's events.

Fires for everyone, not just you

Like chat and projectiles, an event fires for every matching occurrence in the scene (e.g. any NPC's hit, any tracked skill's XP), not only ones involving the local player. Filter inside your handler, or pass the optional id filter (below).

Delivery thread

Callbacks run on the script (worker) thread, drained once per frame (~16 ms), so it is safe to call the rest of the srs.* API from them. A producer on the game/render thread queues the event; the queue is bounded (oldest dropped under a sustained flood). Per-script pause applies — a paused/disabled script stops receiving events; a script inside srs.wait still receives them (events are informational).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Lua Subscribe srs.events.on(name, fn) → token Subscribe with id filter srs.events.on(name, id, fn) → token Unsubscribe srs.events.off(token) → bool

name must be one of the event catalog constants (also in srs.events.EVENTS). An unknown name raises an error — this is deliberate typo protection, so a mistyped event name fails loudly at on() instead of silently never firing. off(token) is safe to call from inside a firing callback; a full script reload clears all subscriptions automatically.

The optional middle id argument filters by the event's primary id (see each event below) — e.g. only a specific skill's XP, or a specific varbit.

docs.title: Event catalog
docs.text:
srs.events.EVENTS exposes the valid names as constants, e.g. srs.events.EVENTS.XP_GAINED == "xpGained". Every payload table also carries an event field (the name) so one handler can dispatch on multiple subscriptions.

Constant Event name XP_GAINED "xpGained" LEVEL_UP "levelUp" INVENTORY_CHANGED "inventoryChanged" VARBIT_CHANGED "varbitChanged" NPC_SPAWNED "npcSpawned" NPC_DESPAWNED "npcDespawned" HITSPLAT "hitsplat"

Catalog

Every event listed below is live. srs.events.EVENTS holds the name constants. Subscribing to a name not in the catalog raises an error (typo protection), as does subscribing to "varbitChanged" without an id.

docs.title: "xpGained"
docs.text:
Fires when a skill's experience increases. The optional id filter is the skill index (see Skill).

Field Type Notes event string "xpGained" skill int Skill index xp int New total experience for the skill gained int Experience delta since the previous tick (> 0) level int Current (real) level of the skill wallClock number Milliseconds when the event was observed

docs.title: "levelUp"
docs.text:
Fires when a skill's real level increases (a genuine level-up, not a boost). The optional id filter is the skill index.

Field Type Notes event string "levelUp" skill int Skill index level int New level previousLevel int Level before the gain wallClock number Milliseconds when the event was observed

No spurious burst on login

The tick-diff producers (xpGained, levelUp, inventoryChanged, npcSpawned / npcDespawned) prime their baseline silently on the first tick they see (and whenever you are logged out), so logging in does not fire an event for every skill / item / on-screen NPC — only genuine changes observed while logged in are delivered.

docs.title: "inventoryChanged"
docs.text:
Fires when your backpack contents change, as a net quantity delta per item id (aggregated across slots, so it is robust to items being reordered between slots — one event per changed item id per tick, not per slot). Optional id filter = item id.

Field Type Notes event string "inventoryChanged" itemId int The item whose total quantity changed quantityDelta int Net change (> 0 gained, < 0 lost) container int Inventory container id (93) slot int -1 — aggregate event, not a per-slot notification wallClock number Milliseconds when the event was observed

A spawn index reused within a single tick for a different NPC id is reported as a despawn of the old followed by a spawn of the new.

Use srs.hitsplats for the full feed

This is a cut-down view. srs.hitsplats carries the same splats with the exact victim resolved (name, NPC id, spawn index, tile, and a live ActionTarget), the game tick, and polling reads (recent / onSelf / onTarget) for scripts that don't want an event handler.

Only 12 (block) and 16 (damage) are supported names; other ids are passed through raw. Branch on the number, not on a name. amount is unaffected and reliable. See Hit splats for the full contract.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
-- Track XP/hr for Woodcutting and shout on a level-up.
local WOODCUTTING = Skill.Woodcutting   -- skill index (see Globals)
local session = 0

-- Filtered subscription: only Woodcutting XP reaches this handler.
srs.events.on(srs.events.EVENTS.XP_GAINED, WOODCUTTING, function(e)
    session = session + e.gained
    log.info(("+%d wc xp (%d total this run)"):format(e.gained, session))
end)

-- Unfiltered: any skill's level-up.
local tok = srs.events.on("levelUp", function(e)
    log.info(("LEVEL UP! skill %d is now %d"):format(e.skill, e.level))
    -- e.event == "levelUp"
end)

-- ... srs.events.off(tok) to stop listening early (optional; reload clears it).

docs.title: Game
docs.text:
srs.game

Engine-level state queries that don't belong on Player or the entity facades. Scripts use this to know whether a login screen is up, whether a logout transition is in flight, or to disambiguate login-failure modes (wrong creds vs. banned vs. not a member) by reading the live login index.

Read-only

Scripts cannot drive the login flow themselves — that's owned by Breaks / BreakManager so credentials stay sandboxed.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Lua Current top-level state srs.game.state() → integer Human-readable label of the current state srs.game.stateName() → string Convenience — state == LoggedIn srs.game.isLoggedIn() → boolean Login sub-state index srs.game.loginIndex() → integer Members world? srs.game.isMembersWorld() → boolean Item display name by id srs.game.itemName(id) → string Full item definition by id srs.defs.item(id) → table

loginIndex is the live login-screen sub-state index. Only meaningful when state() is LoginScreen / LoggingIn. Returns -1 when the index can't be read — in that case the break manager's login driver falls back to widget-based detection.

isMembersWorld is true iff the currently-selected world is a members world. It reads the cached world flags; returns false pre-login, so use state() to tell pre-login apart from an actual F2P world.

itemName resolves an item's in-game display name by id — even for off-screen items the renderer never touched — by invoking the engine's load-on-demand item loader on the engine thread. It blocks briefly (up to ~3 s) while the load completes, falling back to the live cache on timeout, and returns an empty string for id <= 0 or total failure. When the id is already decoded (inventory, bank, equipment, hovered ground) it is answered instantly from the live cache; only a genuine miss pays the wait, so call it from pulse / onTick, never from draw.

srs.defs.item(id) returns the full item metadata behind that name (name, examine, stackable, tradeable, equip slot, value, weight, noted / placeholder links), read straight off the engine's decoded ItemType with no hand-maintained tables. It uses the same resolution as itemName, so the same ~3 s blocking caveat applies: call it from pulse / onTick, never from draw. .valid is false only when the id can't be resolved at all — name may still be non-empty from the cache even then.

Lua lives on srs.defs

The Lua binding is srs.defs.item(id), alongside srs.defs.npc — not srs.game.item*. See Defs for the full field table.

docs.text:
if not srs.game.isLoggedIn() then return end
if srs.game.state() == 25 then return end  -- Loading
doWork()

docs.title: GameObject
docs.text:
srs.gameobject

Query and interact with scene loc objects — game objects, walls, decorations, ground decorations. Distinct from NPCs and players.

Names come from the runtime LocType cache; entries with empty names are nameless decorations (still queryable by id).

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Method Lua All locs (heavy) srs.gameobject.all() → table (1-based list) By id srs.gameobject.byId(id) → table (1-based list) By name srs.gameobject.byName(name) → table (1-based list) Nearest (any) srs.gameobject.nearest() → GameObjectEntry \| nil Nearest by name srs.gameobject.nearestByName(name) → GameObjectEntry \| nil Interact (target + action) srs.gameobject.interact(target, action) → bool Find-nearest-and-interact srs.gameobject.interactNearest(name, action) → bool Interact with first available verb srs.gameobject.interactFirstAvailable(target, actions) → bool Examine srs.gameobject.examine(target) → bool

interactNearest prefers the nearest same-name loc that actually exposes action (skipping decorative twins with no menu), and only falls back to the nearest by name alone if the loc cache hasn't decoded any yet. interact and interactFirstAvailable re-resolve the loc from the entry's tile and plane, so pass an entry from a recent query.

byName / nearestByName are case- and whitespace-insensitive against the in-game display name (e.g. "Bank booth", "bankbooth", and "BANK_BOOTH" all hit the same target).

all() is heavy

all() returns every loc in every loaded scene (all 4 planes). Tens of thousands of rows in a typical city. Prefer the filtered helpers, or filter the result yourself.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
GameObjectEntry (read-only):

Field Type Notes id integer LocType id name string Display name (may be empty for decorations) tileX integer World tile X tileY integer World tile Y plane integer 0..3 actions table of strings Menu-option verbs the loc exposes, in menu order (e.g. {"Mine"}, {"Deposit"}, {"Search"}). These are the exact strings interact accepts. Empty when the LocType isn't cached yet (renderer decodes lazily). A real 1-based table (a copy), safe to keep and iterate with ipairs. rotation integer Placement rotation, 0-3 (one quarter turn each); -1 for wall decorations shape integer LocType shape (0-3 walls, 9 diagonal wall, 10 centrepiece, 11 diagonal centrepiece); -1 for wall decorations orientation integer rotation * 512 (+256 for shape 11), 0-2047; -1 for wall decorations animationId integer Animation the loc is playing; -1 when not animating animationFrame integer Current animation frame; -1 when not animating animationElapsed integer Client cycles (20 ms; 30 per game tick) into the current animation; -1 when not animating animationLength integer Total length of the animation in client cycles; -1 when not animating. Remaining = animationLength - animationElapsed

The actions list removes the need to hardcode or guess verb strings. Read it off any entry to discover what the loc can do, or hand a candidate list to interactFirstAvailable to click whichever verb the loc actually has.

All list returns (all, byId, byName) are real 1-based Lua tables, so type(x) == "table", #x and ipairs all work.

interactFirstAvailable(target, actions) tries each candidate in order and fires the first one the loc exposes (a read-only probe, so only one real click is dispatched — no speculative attempts). Returns the interact result, or false if the loc exposes none of them (or its LocType isn't cached). This replaces the "loop over candidate verbs calling interact until one sticks" pattern.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
-- Chop the nearest tree
srs.gameobject.interactNearest("Tree", "Chop down")

-- Inspect what a loc can do
local box = srs.gameobject.nearestByName("Bank deposit box")
if box then
    for _, verb in ipairs(box.actions) do print(verb) end
    -- Click whichever deposit verb this box exposes
    srs.gameobject.interactFirstAvailable(box, {"Deposit", "Deposit-All", "Bank"})
end

docs.title: Pathfinding / movement
docs.text:
The walk family — game.moveTo, game.walkTo, game.minimapWalkTo, game.walkFastCanvas, game.walkSmart, game.isMoving, game.hasArrived, game.cancelMove — is documented on Walk alongside the newer srs.walk facade. Two functions live only here:

Method Lua Returns Raw path query game.findPath(goalX, goalY) {found, cost, nodesExplored, path={ {x,y}, ... }} \| nil Nearest safe tile game.findSafeTile(originX, originY, dangerTiles[, radius=5[, plane=player plane]]) {x, y, plane, onCanvas, walkable} \| nil

game.findPath runs the client-side pathfinder from the player's position without moving; useful for reachability and cost checks.

game.findSafeTile searches outward in Chebyshev square rings around the origin for the nearest walkable tile not in dangerTiles (a list of {x=, y=, plane=} tables); at equal distance, a tile projectable on the canvas beats an off-canvas one. The origin itself is skipped. Three overloads: (originX, originY, dangerTiles), (…, radius), (…, radius, plane). Returns nil when no candidate within the radius qualifies.

Same search as srs.walk

game.findSafeTile shares its ring-search implementation with the safe-tile search on Walk, so behavior cannot drift between them. The result is a {x, y, plane, onCanvas, walkable} table (or nil when no tile qualifies), and danger entries without a plane key default to the search plane.

docs.text:

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
-- Dodge: step to the nearest safe tile away from two danger tiles
local me = game.playerPosition()
if me then
    local danger = {
        { x = me.x, y = me.y, plane = me.plane },
        { x = me.x + 1, y = me.y, plane = me.plane },
    }
    local safe = game.findSafeTile(me.x, me.y, danger, 4)
    if safe and safe.onCanvas then
        game.walkFastCanvas(safe.x, safe.y)
    elseif safe then
        game.moveTo(safe.x, safe.y)
    else
        log.warn("No safe tile within 4")
    end
end

docs.title: GE Prices
docs.text:
srs.ge

Live Grand Exchange market / guide prices, for pricing offers sensibly.

The native OSRS client has no "your price is far above the guide — are you sure?" dialog, so srs.ge.buyItem / sellItem place whatever price you pass with no safety net. These methods give scripts an independent market reference.

Prices are fetched client-side over HTTPS from the OSRS Wiki real-time API (with a GE-Tracker fallback) and cached per item id for 60 s. Lookups are keyed purely by item id — no login required.

Blocking — never call from draw

The first lookup for an item is a blocking HTTPS round-trip on the calling script thread (subsequent calls within the TTL hit the cache). Call from onTick / pulse / your own logic, never from the draw callback.

Wiki API etiquette

The wiki requires a descriptive User-Agent with a contact. A default is sent; override it with srs.ge.setPriceUserAgent if you distribute a script widely.

docs.title: Prices
docs.text:
itemId <= 0 is always invalid / 0.

Method Lua Full price record srs.ge.prices(itemId) → GePriceInfo Instant-buy price (what you pay now) srs.ge.buyPrice(itemId) → int Instant-sell price (what you get now) srs.ge.sellPrice(itemId) → int Midpoint guide price srs.ge.guidePrice(itemId) → int Adaptive buy price (widen to fill) srs.ge.adaptiveBuyPrice(itemId, retry) → int Adaptive sell price (undercut to fill) srs.ge.adaptiveSellPrice(itemId, retry) → int

Scalar getters return 0 on any failure. Failed lookups are cached for the TTL too, so a failure isn't retried until the TTL expires or you call clearPriceCache(). The adaptive prices start from the instant side and widen the margin by retry (bump it each time an offer fails to fill): margin = 2% + 1% × retry, plus another 3% when traded volume is known and thin (0 < volume < 1000; unknown volume 0 adds nothing). buy = high × (1 + margin), sell = low × (1 − margin) (floored at 1). Use them to re-list more aggressively.

docs.title: Cache / config
docs.text:
Method Lua Set cache TTL (ms; <= 0 disables) srs.ge.setPriceCacheTtlMs(ms) Clear the price cache srs.ge.clearPriceCache() Override the wiki User-Agent srs.ge.setPriceUserAgent(ua)

Lua naming

The price methods share the srs.ge table with the offer methods, so the cache knobs are Price-suffixed in Lua (setPriceCacheTtlMs, clearPriceCache, setPriceUserAgent) to keep them distinct from the offer surface.

docs.title: Types
docs.text:
GePriceInfo — fields are read-only; isValid() / mid() are called with : (p:mid()).

Field Type Meaning itemId integer Item id (−1 if unset) high integer Instant-buy price (gp) — what you pay to buy now low integer Instant-sell price (gp) — what you get selling now volume integer Recent traded volume (0 if the source lacks it) valid boolean true if the lookup succeeded

Helpers: isValid(), mid() (rounded midpoint, falling back to whichever side is populated). high / low follow the wiki's sense — high is the most recent instant-buy, low the most recent instant-sell — so you pay ~high to buy now and receive ~low to sell now.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
local SHARK = 385
local p = srs.ge.prices(SHARK)
if p.valid then
    print(("shark: buy %d / sell %d / guide %d (vol %d)")
        :format(p.high, p.low, p:mid(), p.volume))
end

docs.title: Grand Exchange
docs.text:
srs.ge

Read the player's 8 Grand Exchange offer slots and drive the GE interface.

Offer state is read live and works whether the GE window is open or closed — no open window required. Interaction drives the GE's interface components (offer boxes, steppers, search box) plus keyboard entry for exact numeric / item-name input.

Most interaction needs the GE open

State reads (offers, offer, hasData, the slot predicates) work anywhere. Everything that clicks — createBuyOffer, buyItem, confirm, … — needs the Grand Exchange interface open first. Open it by interacting with a GE clerk: srs.npc.interact(clerk, "Exchange").

Blocking helpers

buyItem / sellItem / setQuantity / setPrice / searchItem drive a multi-step flow with internal sleeps and keyboard entry. They block the calling script thread (up to a few seconds) and mute its pulse / onTick until they return. Blocking is safe, but never call them from draw.

docs.title: State
docs.text:
Valid GE open or closed. slot is 0..7.

Method Lua Any offer data resolved srs.ge.hasData() → bool All 8 slots srs.ge.offers() → table (8 entries, 1-based) One slot srs.ge.offer(slot) → GeOfferInfo First empty slot (−1 if none) srs.ge.firstEmptySlot() → int Slot holding itemId (−1 if none) srs.ge.slotOf(itemId) → int Slot is buying/selling srs.ge.isSlotActive(slot) → bool Slot is finished/cancelled srs.ge.isSlotFinished(slot) → bool Anything collectable srs.ge.anyFinished() → bool Every non-empty slot complete srs.ge.allComplete() → bool

docs.text:
Method Lua GE window or standalone collection box open srs.ge.isOpen() → bool GE offers interface open (overview or setup) srs.ge.isOfferScreenOpen() → bool

isOfferScreenOpen is true on the 8-box overview as well as the setup screen, and is the precondition buyItem / sellItem check. isOpen additionally returns true for the standalone collection box opened from the bank.

docs.title: Collection & navigation
docs.text:
Method Lua Collect finished offers to inventory srs.ge.collectToInventory() → bool Collect to bank (collection box only) srs.ge.collectToBank() → bool Open an active offer's detail screen srs.ge.openSlot(slot) → bool Abort an active offer (detail screen must be open) srs.ge.abort(slot) → bool Collect one box of the open detail screen srs.ge.collectSlot([asNotes=true]) → bool Close the GE window srs.ge.close() → bool Compat no-op — always false srs.ge.back() → bool

collectToInventory prefers the GE-screen "Collect to inventory" button and falls back to the standalone collection box. abort requires the offer's detail screen open first (openSlot(slot), wait a tick) — the "Abort offer" button lives on the detail screen, not the overview. It is dispatched directly against that button; a synthesized mouse click on it silently no-ops.

collectSlot collects one box of the open detail screen per call — the items box or the coins box (refund after an abort, or sale proceeds). It reads the box's own op list and prefers Collect-notes for unstackables when asNotes is true (default), so bought items land in the backpack as a single noted stack; the coins box uses its own collect op. Call it every tick until offer(slot) reads Empty — the engine drops back to the overview by itself once the slot is drained. Returns false when nothing collectable is shown (detail screen not open, or already empty).

-- Abort a stalled buy, then take the refund + partial fill.
if srs.ge.isSlotActive(slot) then
    srs.ge.openSlot(slot)             -- tick 1: detail screen
    -- tick 2:
    srs.ge.abort(slot)
else
    -- tick 3+: slot is Cancelled — drain it
    if srs.ge.offer(slot).state ~= srs.ge.State.Empty then srs.ge.collectSlot() end
end

There is no "back" button on the native GE — the engine returns to the overview automatically after confirm / abort / collect, so back() exists only for API compatibility and always returns false; use close() to leave.

docs.text:
